rationale: Background EEG amplitude and spectra vary a lot between neonates. With only absolute features, a seizure in a low-voltage baby can look like normal background in a high-voltage baby. I'll add a robust per-recording z-score of every feature: subtract the recording's median and divide by its IQR. This uses no labels and is computed within each recording, so the classifier sees how much each second departs from that neonate's own background. The absolute features stay in alongside the new ones.

I'm switching from the referential recording to the 18-channel bipolar double-banana montage used clinically, filtered to 0.5–30 Hz, and leaving the features, classifier and smoothing unchanged. The shared reference electrode blurs and spreads focal neonatal seizures across all channels. The bipolar derivations remove that and pick out local rhythmic discharges. The band-pass also stops drift and muscle noise from inflating line length and RMS.

Neonatal seizures are rhythmic, evolving discharges. The current features only measure amplitude and band power, so a seizure can look the same as a high-amplitude artifact or background burst. I'm adding four per-channel rhythmicity features, each summarised as max and median over channels: the autocorrelation peak after the first zero crossing (computed from the 0.5–15 Hz power spectrum), the fraction of power in the dominant 0.5 Hz peak bin, the peak frequency, and normalized spectral entropy. These should separate seizures from non-rhythmic high-energy activity.

Neonatal seizures last tens of seconds to minutes and evolve over time, while artifacts and background bursts are brief. The classifier currently sees only one 8 s window per second. This change adds temporal context: centred moving means of all 20 features over 15 s and 61 s windows, computed within each recording and without labels. That lets the model pick up sustained rhythmic activity and tell it apart from short transients.

Right now the raw referential signal goes straight into the features with no filtering. Slow drift inflates RMS and delta power, and 50 Hz mains plus muscle noise dominate line length, so the max-over-channels amplitude features mostly track artifacts. This change band-passes each channel at 0.5–30 Hz once per recording (zero-phase 4th-order Butterworth, one channel at a time to keep memory bounded) before the unchanged windowed features. The amplitude and line-length features should then reflect EEG-band seizure activity rather than noise.

The current context features average the over-channel maximum, and that maximum can come from a different channel every second. A neonatal seizure is focal and stays rhythmic in the same channel, while artifacts and background bursts flicker across channels. So I'm adding per-channel persistence features: each channel's 10 features are averaged over centred 15 s and 61 s windows first, and only then is the max over channels taken. This captures sustained, spatially consistent rhythmic activity. The existing features, classifier and smoothing stay the same.

Neonatal seizures are focal, so I'm swapping the single global classifier for a per-channel detector, which the brief lists as an open question. Each training row is one second on one channel. It holds that channel's 10 features, the same features minus their median across channels (how much the channel stands out), and that channel's 15 s and 61 s moving means. The current global max/median and context features are appended so the model keeps the overall picture. The second's label goes to all 19 channels, as in Tapani's per-channel SVM. Each second's prediction is the highest channel probability, then the existing 10 s smoothing. To keep CV time and memory bounded, training uses every 5th second; neighbouring seconds overlap heavily, so little is lost. I haven't run it, so I don't know its Dev score yet.

I'm replacing the 19 referential channels with the 18-channel bipolar double-banana montage (Fp1-F7…Cz-Pz). The features, the per-channel detector, the max over channels and the smoothing stay the same. The shared reference spreads a focal discharge across every channel, which blurs the focality and per-channel persistence features the per-channel model now depends on. Bipolar derivations pick out local rhythmic activity. Round 2 tried this montage with amplitude-only global features, before rhythmicity, per-channel rows or temporal context existed, so this tests the montage again on the current per-channel pipeline. I haven't run it, so I don't know its Dev score yet.

Neonatal seizures are focal, but the current model labels all 19 channels as seizure for every seizure second. Most of those positive rows are uninvolved, background-looking channels, which is label noise, and the prediction step only uses the max over channels anyway. This change adds a multiple-instance relabelling step. A first model ranks the channels within each training seizure second; only the top 4 channels stay as positives and the rest are dropped; a second model is then retrained so the per-channel detector learns real ictal morphology, which matches the max-over-channels prediction step. I haven't run it, so I don't know its Dev score yet.

Right now each second's score is the maximum of 19 noisy per-second channel probabilities, and that maximum is pushed upward in seizure-free seconds of artifact-heavy neonates. Since a neonatal seizure stays rhythmic in the same channel for tens of seconds, I'll smooth each channel's probability over a centred 10 s window before taking the maximum, and keep the existing 10 s smoothing of the output. That should cut false positives from brief single-channel spikes and keep sustained focal detections.

Right now a fixed 10 s moving average and a max over channels turn channel probabilities into the per-second score. Because AUROC is computed on all neonates' seconds together, artifact-heavy neonates with a high baseline cost the most. This change adds a learned second stage. Three grouped inner-CV models produce out-of-fold channel-probability traces on the training recordings. A second gradient-boosting model learns from summaries of those traces: max, top-3 and mean over channels, means over 5–301 s windows, moving maxima, and recording-level quantiles of the max probability as a per-neonate baseline. It should keep sustained, evolving focal detections and suppress each neonate's chronic false-positive level.

I'm adding three waveform-shape features per channel that the current feature set lacks: Hjorth mobility, Hjorth complexity and log mean Teager–Kaiser nonlinear energy, all used in the classic neonatal detectors (Temko, Tapani). Neonatal seizures are regular, spike/sharp-wave discharges with smooth waveforms (low Hjorth complexity) and high instantaneous energy, while background and artifacts are irregular, so these should separate rhythmic ictal waveforms from high-energy non-ictal activity. They pass through the existing focality, persistence, global and context pipeline. Feature count goes from 120 to 156, which increases training time and memory, and I haven't run it, so I don't know the Dev score or whether it stays inside the 25-minute limit.

The training rows are highly correlated: 19 channels per second, overlapping 8 s windows and 15/61 s moving means. The default leaf size of 20 rows lets the gradient booster memorize single moments in single neonates, which hurts when it is scored on unseen neonates. I'm raising the minimum leaf size to 1000 rows and adding L2 regularization, so each split has to describe a pattern spread across many seconds, channels and neonates. The features and post-processing stay the same.

Background EEG differs greatly between neonates and between electrodes, so I'm adding 10 new features per channel: each channel's 10 features minus that channel's median over the whole recording. Median subtraction of log features gives a ratio. This uses no labels and is computed within each recording, so the per-channel detector sees how far a channel moves from its own baseline. Round 1 failed with a noisier version of this idea on the old global model: a median/IQR z-score of global features, at a time when only amplitude features existed. This version is per-channel and median-only, and the absolute features stay in. I haven't run it, so I don't know its Dev score yet.

Every current feature lives in 0.5–30 Hz. That means the model can't see muscle/EMG artifacts (power above 30 Hz) or movement/electrode drift (power below 0.5 Hz), even though these inflate line length, RMS and delta power and raise the max-over-channels baseline in artifact-heavy neonates. I'm adding two log artifact-band powers per channel, 0.1–0.5 Hz and 30–70 Hz. They go through the existing focality, persistence, global and context pipeline so the detector can learn to discount high-energy activity that isn't seizure. Unlike round 5, the signal itself isn't filtered.

Right now the per-channel smoothing and the output smoothing are both fixed at 10 s. Neonatal seizures last tens of seconds to minutes, so the best smoothing length depends on how long seizures last and how noisy the classifier's per-second output is. This change picks both lengths using grouped 3-fold inner CV on the training neonates only. Three inner models give out-of-fold channel probabilities, and the (per-channel, output) window pair with the best concatenated AUROC on those is used for the test predictions. The current 10 s / 10 s setting is one of the options.

Right now each second's score is the maximum over 19 channels. A single bad electrode (electrode pop, a movement spike on one lead) can push that maximum up, while a real neonatal seizure usually involves a few neighbouring electrodes for tens of seconds. This change adds a third option to the existing grouped inner-CV smoothing search: how to combine channels, choosing the mean of the top k channel probabilities for k in {1, 2, 3, 5}, where k=1 is the current max. The out-of-fold probabilities are already computed, so the extra cost is small. I haven't run it, so I don't know its Dev score yet.

Each channel's row will also carry the average of its scalp neighbours' current features (8-connected 10-20 grid). The aim is to separate seizures that spread to nearby electrodes from artifacts on a single electrode, such as an electrode pop or a movement spike on one lead. The current focality feature only compares a channel with the median over all channels, so it cannot tell these two cases apart. This adds 12 columns, the same total as round 12, which ran within the time limit; I haven't run this version, so its Dev score is unknown.

Concatenated AUROC suffers when a seizure-free neonate with many artifacts has high probabilities throughout the recording. This change adds a per-recording output baseline: subtract alpha times a low quantile (25th or 50th percentile) of the recording's own final score. Alpha and the quantile are chosen together with the existing smoothing and top-k settings by the grouped inner CV, and alpha=0 (the current behaviour) is one of the options. It uses no labels and is computed within each recording. Unlike rounds 1 and 14, it normalizes the classifier output, not the features. I haven't run it, so I don't know its Dev score yet; the extra search cost is small.

Some neonates in this cohort have long seizures or near-continuous status epilepticus that run for several minutes. The longest per-channel persistence window is 61 s, so it can't tell a channel that stays rhythmic for minutes from shorter artifact or background episodes. I'm adding a third per-channel persistence scale of 181 s. It adds 12 per-channel and 12 global max-over-channel columns and changes nothing else.
